It is worth noting that these beginnings appeared alongside the successive stages in the crisis of bourgeois philosophy. Consider the significance of the following events:
Immediately after the First World War, a number of bourgeois philosophers visited countries of the East.
In 1921, John Dewey published Letters from China and Japan. Other Western philosophers published a number of similar books.
In 1922, Bertrand Russell published The Problem of China after visiting the country.

In these works and others like them, their authors repeatedly argued that the values of the East could help the West overcome its philosophical crisis. This idea appears in writers such as Bergson, Russell, Dewey, Riecken, Petro, and others.

After the Second World War, the issue was raised much more sharply. International philosophical conferences were held in Hawaii and Honolulu, with active participation from many leading contemporary idealist philosophers. Some attended in person, while others sent papers and reports. Dewey was a regular participant. Others included Sidney Hook, one of the leading American idealist philosophers and among the most reactionary; Radhakrishnan and Raju from India; Suzuki from Japan; Sharif from Pakistan; and Charles Malik from Lebanon.

At more than one of these conferences, these philosophers discussed in detail the idea of merging Eastern and Western philosophy. They also suggested that if Marxists wanted to develop Marxism further, they too should turn to the East and incorporate teachings drawn from Eastern values.

One striking feature of this trend is that petty-bourgeois thinkers in Asia and Africa have been among the strongest advocates of merging Marxism with Eastern philosophy. Why? Two opposing reasons come together dialectically. First, they find a number of attractive elements in Marxism. Second, like other sections of the petty bourgeoisie around the world, they are afraid of Marxism in its genuine form. They therefore propose what is called an “Eastern Marxism.”
Whatever we think of this proposal, it raises several questions:
Can the traditional and contemporary philosophies of Eastern countries enter into active interaction with contemporary world bourgeois philosophy and have a productive influence on it?
Must such influence necessarily lead to the creation of a merged Eastern-Western philosophy?
Can Eastern philosophy influence Marxism? And would that influence take the form of a merger?
We can answer these questions, in the same order, as follows.

Even under capitalism, the conditions are developing for greater unity across the world. Modern communications make the world smaller and, in practice, reduce the isolation of what might once have been regarded as the world’s distant “countryside.” As communist relations develop, this process of unification becomes faster.

Under such conditions, cultural unification will naturally become broader and deeper. The cultures of different peoples and continents will move closer together, and cultural cooperation and interaction will become increasingly urgent, especially in intellectual and philosophical work. This process will speed up as social relations develop more rapidly in different countries.

As development accelerates in these countries and deep social changes take place, cultural development will also change. Contemporary philosophy in these countries will naturally develop a character of its own.

When this philosophy begins to raise questions that are not purely local but broader and more universal, it will inevitably influence Western philosophy. We can already see signs of this today. Over the last fifteen or twenty years, hundreds of studies on Eastern philosophy have appeared in Western Europe and America. Some ideas from these philosophies will inevitably spread beyond specialist circles and enter ordinary thought.
But this does not mean that Eastern and Western philosophy will merge into a single philosophy. Such a merger is not realistic.

Idealist philosophers have already tried to bring it about. In 1949, the Second East-West Philosophers’ Conference was held in Honolulu. Some expected its participants to agree on a formula for combining selected elements from both sides into a single Eastern-Western philosophy—a kind of philosophical Esperanto.
But the expectation that such an artificial agreement could succeed was itself an idealist illusion.
Philosophy is a product of the historical development of human societies. The advocates of philosophical merger ignored this fact. They also ignored the class character of philosophy.

They further ignored the fact that Eastern philosophy can influence Western philosophy only through a natural historical process shaped by the development of Eastern societies themselves. Conscious social activity can speed up or slow down this process, but it cannot be produced through some artificial operation imposed from outside. A natural historical process does not happen simply because a group of philosophers decides that it should.
Attempts to create an agreed philosophical merger by arbitrary selection can therefore produce only an eclectic philosophy, dominated by the idealist elements of the philosophies being combined.
The idea of merging Marxist philosophy with Eastern philosophy is even further removed from reality.

Marxism itself has no need for this kind of artificial merger. If Marxism is to spread to new countries and become useful and practically applicable in the countries of the East, what it needs above all is a precise understanding of the concrete conditions of each individual country. That matters far more than merging Marxism with the philosophies of those countries.

But this does not mean that Marxism cannot develop by drawing on elements from Eastern cultures. It means that, as Marxism is applied to the concrete conditions of each country, it will develop through its engagement with those elements.

Take, for example, the well-known Marxist theory of historical socio-economic formations. If we apply this theory to the development of Eastern countries when analysing their history, we will inevitably encounter new phenomena, such as the Asiatic mode of production.
Further research into this question must in turn enrich Marxist-Leninist theory concerning socio-economic formations.

What does the study of Asian societies from the standpoint of this theory require? Above all, it requires us to begin from the actual social activity of the countries of Asia. That is the basic way to approach the problem.
In any case, we can already reach one conclusion. Marxist philosophy is not a fixed doctrine. It is a guide to action. Every Marxist teaching is therefore capable of development.

The cultures and philosophies of the East are among the sources through which such development can take place when Marxism is applied to real social relations. They can contribute new forms and insights that make Marxism richer and more productive.

Studying the intellectual heritage of the East—including the Arab-Islamic heritage—in relation to its social and economic foundation and according to the Marxist method of research is one form of precisely this kind of application.
Third — This is the third trend in Western Orientalist studies of the heritage.

This trend concentrates on the most conservative and reactionary aspects of that heritage, especially those most deeply immersed in the supernatural and the realm of the absolute. At the same time, it obscures the aspects that contain materialist tendencies, or hides the social dimensions that can exist even within apparently supernatural forms, as we find in the philosophical Sufism of figures such as al-Ḥallāj and the martyred al-Suhrawardī.

Many Orientalists have even tried to reinterpret the philosophical systems of thinkers such as al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, and Ibn Rushd in ways that remove their materialist dimensions. The result is to turn them into purely Sufi, Illuminationist, or religious systems.
We find one example in Carra de Vaux, in his treatment of Sufi terminology in al-Fārābī’s writings.

Carra de Vaux tries to show that this terminology is a dominant feature of al-Fārābī’s philosophy. He then uses this supposed feature to pull these terms away from their rational philosophical content and to cast doubt on al-Fārābī’s place within the rationalist tradition.

Yet a systematic scientific study shows that rationalism is the defining character of al-Fārābī’s philosophy as a whole, whether we look at his theory of knowledge, his philosophy of existence, or his social philosophy.
Massignon followed a similar path by placing al-Kindī, al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, and other Islamic philosophers among the Sufis.

We find the same tendency in Gilson, who regards Ibn Sīnā as the founder of the theory of Illumination. The Danish Orientalist Mehren also paid particular attention to Ibn Sīnā’s mystical writings, publishing and translating them.
This brings us to a problem that occupied an extraordinary number of pages in the writings of many of these Orientalists: the supposed Illuminationist mysticism of Ibn Sīnā.
The whole problem begins with a passing phrase at the start of Ibn Ṭufayl’s introduction to his famous philosophical story Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān.
Ibn Ṭufayl begins his introduction by saying:
“You asked me, dear and loyal brother, ... to share with you as much as I can of the secrets of the mashriqī wisdom mentioned by the Master Abū ʿAlī Ibn Sīnā.”

Elsewhere in the introduction, Ibn Ṭufayl reports something Ibn Sīnā had said in the introduction to The Healing. The point is that The Healing was written according to the Peripatetic school, while Ibn Sīnā’s own true position, he says, should be sought in another work, his al-Falsafa al-Mashriqiyya.
It was the word mashriqiyya in these two passages, attributed to Ibn Sīnā, that created the problem for the Orientalists.
The question was how the first vowel should be pronounced. Should the word be read with a u sound—mushriqiyya—or with an a sound—mashriqiyya?
The difficulty was that Ibn Sīnā’s book bearing this title, al-Ḥikma al-Mashriqiyya or al-Falsafa al-Mashriqiyya, had not survived in a form available to them.

For these scholars, the question was extremely important because changing that single vowel produced two very different meanings. Read with the u sound, the expression meant Illuminationist wisdom. Read with the a sound, it meant Eastern wisdom or Eastern philosophy.
If the first meaning could be established, they could then argue that Ibn Sīnā was an Illuminationist, in a sense connected with Sufism.
So this was not merely a question about a word. For Western bourgeois Orientalists, much more was at stake.
It mattered greatly to them that the book Ibn Sīnā supposedly regarded as the true expression of his own position, rather than The Healing, should turn out to be an Illuminationist work.

That would remove Ibn Sīnā once and for all from the camp of defenders of Aristotelian rationalism and place him instead among the irrational, metaphysical Illuminationists associated with al-Suhrawardī.

It would also change how his position on the primacy of existence could be understood, at least in the theory of knowledge. One might still speak of such a position among some Peripatetic philosophers, but not in relation to the “real” Ibn Sīnā—the author of Illuminationist Wisdom, whose leading principle would then have to be the primacy of essence.

For bourgeois ideology—and still more for imperialist ideology—what matters in our age is not to uncover, in the brightest parts of our intellectual heritage, philosophical teachings that point toward the materialist tendency contained in the idea of the primacy of existence. It is far more useful to present that heritage to us stamped with the seal of “Illuminationist lights,” deepening our alienation in the modern world.

This is why we say that the enormous effort spent by so many Western Orientalists trying to establish a u sound in the first syllable of mushriqiyya, in the title of a lost book by Ibn Sīnā, was not pointless. It was not wordplay. It was not a storm in a teacup, as some might imagine.
It was another expression of their ideological approach.

Some of them therefore went beyond the question of the vowel itself. Even if the word were read with the a sound, meaning “Eastern,” they still tried to classify Ibn Sīnā’s unseen book as an Illuminationist or “spiritualist” work.
Western Orientalists’ strong attraction to the Sufi currents in our heritage brings us to another phenomenon. At first sight, it seems like one of the strangest contradictions in Orientalism.

We have already seen an Orientalist tendency that puts a natural or racial barrier between Eastern and Western thought and builds whole theories to strengthen and defend that barrier—the theory of race and the theory of philosophical centrality.
Now we encounter what appears to be its complete opposite.
One Orientalist treats the “Islamic Sufi heritage” as a “bridge between Eastern and Western religious thought.”

He describes Islamic Sufis as speaking the language of a universal mysticism. To prove this “universal” character, he draws a series of comparisons: Judaism, Christianity, Gnosticism, and Neoplatonism in the West; and Indian, Buddhist, and Persian teachings in the East.
He also tries to find similarities between Qurʾānic verses, interpreted mystically, and statements made by mystics in both East and West.
He imagines scholars asking what could explain the resemblance “between the traditions of Sufism and Western mystics on the one hand, and Eastern thought on the other.”
In the case of some learned Sufis, such as al-Ghazālī, he finds one possible explanation. Some travelled widely and came into contact with “thinkers from other traditions and cultural settings.”
But he then argues that this cannot explain the “striking similarities between the experiences of Sufis and those of Christian saints separated from one another by time and place.”
At this point, he turns to a purely supernatural explanation.

He says that while some things in Sufism can be learned through study, “what remains cannot be learned through study or words.” He supports this claim by referring to another Western writer on mysticism, Underhill, and to the Muslim Sufi Abū Ṭālib al-Makkī (d. 996), who said that a person with spiritual knowledge has no need of a book. Such a person learns what he knows from his master, God, who teaches him to read the book of life.
He then draws on Carl Jung’s idea of the “collective unconscious” and Emerson’s idea of “a mind common to all human beings.”

From all this he concludes that approaching mysticism, whether Christian or Indian, allows us to see that the similarities in mystical practice and in the basic truth of these teachings support the idea that God is present everywhere and “opens every door that leads people to Him.”
Finally, he arrives confidently at this conclusion:
“With this understanding, it is easy to see that whether we approach the bridge from its Western side or its Eastern side, we will meet, just as the common light and truth will meet.”
Is it really a contradiction that Orientalism contains these two apparently opposite tendencies?
In rational thought, we are told, East and West cannot meet. Yet in mystical and supernatural thought, they can meet and become one world.
From the standpoint of imperialist and bourgeois ideology, this is a contradiction only on the surface. At a deeper level, the two tendencies fit both ideologies perfectly well.

Ideologically, it is useful to unite East and West around supernatural thought, around the glorification of illiteracy, and around the idea of learning from a “book of life” that is not the real life of human beings.
And it is just as useful, ideologically, to insist on an absolute separation between East and West whenever thought is rooted in social reality.
Otherwise, why draw such a sharp line between rational and irrational thought?
Both have a history. Neither arose or lived outside history—the history of human beings, which means the history of human social activity.

The basic purpose of all these positions is to hide anything in intellectual life that points toward a relationship with the reality of class struggle as a force shaping the direction of human history.
Fourth — The positive trend in Orientalist studies of the Eastern heritage.
Although the three trends discussed above have dominated Orientalist studies, their dominance has never been complete.
Important Orientalist works have departed from them and approached the Eastern heritage from positions closer to objective study than to the partisan outlook shaped by imperialist ideology.

Some of these more positive studies have even been based on a sound historical outlook or a scientific method. This trend includes both bourgeois Orientalists and Marxist Orientalists and researchers.
Among the first group, one scholar especially worth mentioning is the French scholar Paul Masson-Oursel and his scientific historical study of ancient Eastern philosophy.

His study stands out for its systematic method. The facts he presents challenge the very foundation on which the theory of philosophical centrality was built. His work begins from a sound theoretical understanding of the basic unity of human thought.
At the beginning of his introduction, Masson-Oursel writes:

“No one today can believe that the Greeks, the Romans, and the peoples of medieval and modern Europe were the only masters of philosophical thought. In other parts of humanity, several centres of abstract thought also appeared. Their light shone clearly and spread across the world. And since these centres were not isolated from one another, as people once thought, we must recognize that Western thought cannot be understood by itself. Its historical explanation requires us to place it again within the wider human setting, because true history is the unity of world history.”
He applies this method throughout his study.
